items.title: E100 Curcumin
items.summary: Curcumin is the yellow pigment of turmeric. EFSA set a safe daily intake in 2010 but said some lab genotoxicity findings were not fully settled.
cautions: People with liver, gall bladder or bile duct problems, and anyone taking medicines, when using curcumin supplements. This concerns supplements, not the small amounts used as a colour.
sources: UK COT committee. Statement on curcumin in food supplements

items.title: E101 Riboflavin
items.summary: Riboflavin is vitamin B2. EFSA found no genotoxicity concern and no adverse effects in the animal studies it reviewed.

items.title: E102 Tartrazine
items.summary: Linked to a small rise in hyperactive behaviour in some children when eaten in colour mixtures. The evidence is mixed, and regulators have kept a safe daily intake.
cautions: Children, and families who notice a link between brightly coloured foods and behaviour. The EU label rule names children's activity and attention.
sources: EFSA. Re-evaluation of tartrazine (E 102), 2009

items.title: E1105 Lysozyme
items.summary: Made from hen's egg white. EFSA said in 2011 that lysozyme in wine may trigger allergic reactions in egg-allergic people.
cautions: People with egg allergy. EFSA and EU labelling rules treat egg-derived lysozyme as an allergen.
sources: EFSA NDA Panel. Lysozyme labelling opinion, EFSA Journal 2011

items.title: E120 Carmine
items.summary: Carmine is a red dye made from crushed cochineal insects. It can cause allergic reactions in some people, occasionally severe.
cautions: People with allergies to carmine or cochineal, and possibly people with insect allergies. Vegans and vegetarians avoid it for ethical reasons.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of cochineal, carminic acid, carmines (E 120) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2015

items.summary: EFSA's 2021 review found no safety concern at reported uses and no need for a numerical daily limit.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of polydextrose (E 1200) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2021

items.title: E1201 Polyvinylpyrrolidone
items.summary: PVP is a synthetic polymer used in tablets and supplements. EFSA found no safety concern.

EU. Commission Regulation (EU) 2025/1337

items.title: E1202 Polyvinylpolypyrrolidone

items.title: E128 Red 2G
items.summary: Suspended in the EU in 2007 after EFSA raised a cancer concern about aniline, a substance the body can form from it. It is not an approved food colour.

items.title: E131 Patent blue V
items.summary: EFSA lowered its safe daily intake in 2013. At maximum permitted levels, toddlers and children with high intake could exceed it, so it is worth keeping to a small part of the diet.
sources: EFSA. Re-evaluation of Patent Blue V (E 131) as a food additive, 2013

items.title: E132 Indigo carmine
items.summary: EFSA confirmed a safe daily intake of 5 mg per kg of body weight in 2014 and again in 2023, after a study checking an earlier worry about the testes did not repeat it.
sources: EFSA. Follow-up of the re-evaluation of indigo carmine (E 132), 2023
EFSA. Re-evaluation of indigo carmine (E 132), 2014

items.title: E133 Brilliant blue FCF
items.summary: EFSA set a safe daily intake of 6 mg per kg of body weight in 2010. Intake was under it in the refined estimate.
sources: EFSA. Re-evaluation of brilliant blue FCF (E 133), 2010
California OEHHA. Health effects assessment: potential neurobehavioral effects of synthetic food dyes in children, 2021
CSPI. Chemical Cuisine: artificial colorings (synthetic food dyes)

items.title: E140 Chlorophylls

sources: EFSA. Re-evaluation of chlorophylls and copper complexes (EFSA Journal, 2015)
EFSA. Update on the working group on re-evaluation, July 2026 (annex)

items.summary: JECFA set an ADI of 0 to 20 mg per kg of body weight. EFSA has not completed its own re-evaluation, so this is an older safety picture.

JECFA evaluation (INCHEM), second record

items.title: E150a Plain caramel colour
items.summary: Plain caramel is made by heating sugar without ammonia or sulfites. It sits under EFSA's group safe intake for caramel colours.

items.title: E150b Caustic sulfite caramel colour
items.summary: Made with sulfites but no ammonia. It sits under EFSA's group safe intake, with estimated intake below it.
cautions: People with sulfite-sensitive asthma may want to check labels.
sources: EFSA. Scientific Opinion on the re-evaluation of caramel colours (E 150 a,b,c,d) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2011
EFSA. Caramel colours reviewed (news release). EFSA, 2011
EFSA. Caramel colours: consumer exposure lower than previously estimated. EFSA, 2012

items.summary: EFSA gave this type its own lower safe daily intake because of uncertainty about immune effects. It can contain 4-MEI, which IARC lists as possibly carcinogenic from animal studies.

items.title: E1520 Propylene glycol
items.summary: EFSA's 2018 re-evaluation kept the safe daily intake at 25 mg per kg of body weight. It is not antifreeze (that is ethylene glycol).
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of propane-1,2-diol (E 1520) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2018

items.title: E1521 Polyethylene glycol
items.summary: PEG is a synthetic polymer with older ADIs. EFSA's 2018 exposure assessment found estimated intake near the range of those ADIs.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Refined exposure assessment of polyethylene glycol (E 1521) from its use as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2018
IPCS INCHEM. JECFA evaluation: polyethylene glycols

items.title: E153 Vegetable carbon
items.summary: A black colour made from burnt plant material. EFSA reviewed it in 2012 and again in 2026 to tighten limits on impurities.
sources: EFSA. Scientific opinion on the amendment of the specifications for vegetable carbon (E 153) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2026

items.title: E155 Brown HT
items.summary: EFSA halved its safe daily intake in 2010 to 1.5 mg per kg of body weight. A later estimate still showed high-intake groups above it in some scenarios.
sources: EFSA. EFSA publishes safety assessments of three food colours (news), 2010

items.title: E160a Carotenes
items.summary: Beta-carotene from food use is not a concern for the general population. High-dose supplements have raised lung cancer rates in smokers.
cautions: Smokers and people exposed to asbestos should be cautious about high-dose beta-carotene supplements. This is about supplements, not colour use.
sources: EFSA. Re-evaluation of mixed carotenes (E 160a(i)) and beta-carotene (E 160a(ii)). EFSA Journal, 2012
EFSA. Statement on the safety of beta-carotene use in heavy smokers. EFSA Journal, 2012
CSPI. Chemical Cuisine: beta-carotene

items.title: E160b Annatto
items.summary: Annatto comes from seeds of the achiote tree. EFSA set low safe intakes in 2016. Some children's intakes of norbixin may exceed it, and allergy cases have been reported.
cautions: Toddlers and children with high intakes (per EFSA), and people with a known annatto allergy or chronic hives.
sources: EFSA. Exposure assessment of annatto colouring principles bixin and norbixin (E 160b). EFSA Journal, 2019
Anaphylaxis to annatto dye: a case report. Ann Allergy, 1991
An allergy to goldfish? Highlighting labeling laws for food additives. World Allergy Organ J

items.title: E160c Paprika extract
items.summary: A colour from red peppers. EFSA re-evaluated it in 2015. We could not retrieve the details, so the evidence here is thin.
sources: JECFA/IPCS. Paprika oleoresin evaluation

items.title: E160d Lycopene
items.summary: The red pigment of tomatoes. EFSA set an ADI of 0.5 mg per kg of body weight, lower than JECFA's view of no limit needed.
sources: BfR. EFSA opinion on the safety of lycopene oleoresin from tomatoes

items.title: E160e Beta-apo-8'-carotenal
items.summary: A carotenoid colour. EFSA first set a very low ADI, then raised it sixfold after re-reading the same kidney slides.
sources: EFSA. Re-evaluation of beta-apo-8'-carotenal (E 160e) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2012

items.title: E161b Lutein
items.summary: A yellow pigment from marigold flowers. EFSA set an ADI of 1 mg per kg of body weight in 2010.
sources: EFSA. Statement on the safety assessment of the exposure to lutein preparations based on new data on use levels. 2011

items.title: E162 Beetroot red
items.summary: A red pigment from beetroot. It is a food-derived colour and no credible safety signal was found.
sources: EFSA. Re-evaluation of beetroot red (E 162) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2015 (listing)
JECFA/IPCS. Beet red evaluation

items.title: E163 Anthocyanins

sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of anthocyanins (E 163) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2013
WHO JECFA database. Grape skin extract

items.title: E170 Calcium carbonate
items.summary: EFSA found no safety concern at food-additive levels in 2011 and again in 2023 for infant foods. It is also a common calcium supplement and antacid.
sources: EFSA. Scientific opinion on re-evaluation of calcium carbonate (E 170) as a food additive, 2011
EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of calcium carbonate (E 170) as a food additive in foods for infants below 16 weeks of age, 2023

items.title: E171 Titanium dioxide
items.summary: In 2021 EFSA concluded it can no longer be considered safe as a food additive, because a risk of DNA damage could not be ruled out. No harm has been shown in people.

EFSA. Safety assessment of titanium dioxide (E171) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2021

JECFA. Iron oxide black evaluation (INCHEM)

items.summary: EFSA said in 2016 and again in 2025 that data were too limited to conclude it is safe, especially for its tiny-particle (nano) form.

items.summary: Food-grade carrageenan passed EFSA's 2018 review, but large French cohort studies linked higher intake to more cancer and type 2 diabetes, and animal and cell studies show gut inflammation. EFSA also asked for more infant data.
cautions: Infants: EFSA's first opinion excluded very young infants and asked for more data. People with inflammatory bowel disease sometimes choose to avoid it, although We found no regulator advice to do so.

items.title: E425 Konjac
items.summary: EFSA's 2017 review accepted konjac at current uses but noted a limited toxicity database. Konjac jelly sweets are a choking risk.

items.title: E426 Soybean hemicellulose

cautions: People with soy allergy may want to check labels.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of soybean hemicellulose (E 426) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2017
EU. Commission Regulation (EU) 2020/279

items.title: E427 Cassia gum

sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of sorbitan monostearate (E 491), tristearate (E 492), monolaurate (E 493), monooleate (E 494) and monopalmitate (E 495). EFSA Journal, 2017

items.title: E500 Sodium carbonates
items.summary: Includes ordinary baking soda. Regulators set no numerical limit, and we found no credible safety signal.
sources: EFSA. Scientific opinion on re-evaluation of calcium carbonate (E 170) as a food additive (notes the 1990 SCF group ADI 'not specified' for carbonates), 2011
Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/141 (recitals on sodium and potassium carbonates, SCF 1990)

items.title: E501 Potassium carbonates
items.summary: Regulators set no numerical limit for potassium carbonates, and we found no credible safety signal.
sources: EFSA. Scientific opinion on re-evaluation of calcium carbonate (E 170) as a food additive (notes the 1990 SCF group ADI 'not specified' for carbonates), 2011
Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/141 (recitals on sodium and potassium carbonates, SCF 1990)

items.title: E503 Ammonium carbonates
items.summary: Ammonium carbonates break down into gases when baked, so little remains in the finished food. We found no credible safety signal.
sources: EFSA. Scientific opinion on re-evaluation of calcium carbonate (E 170) as a food additive (notes the 1990 SCF group ADI 'not specified' for carbonates), 2011
Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/141 (recitals on sodium and potassium carbonates, SCF 1990)

items.title: E504 Magnesium carbonates
items.summary: Magnesium carbonates have no numerical limit set by regulators, and we found no credible safety signal.
sources: EFSA. Scientific opinion on re-evaluation of calcium carbonate (E 170) as a food additive (notes the 1990 SCF group ADI 'not specified' for carbonates), 2011
Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/141 (recitals on sodium and potassium carbonates, SCF 1990)

items.title: E507 Hydrochloric acid
items.summary: Hydrochloric acid is used in small amounts in processing and ends up as chloride salts. EFSA saw no safety concern.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of hydrochloric acid (E 507), potassium chloride (E 508), calcium chloride (E 509) and magnesium chloride (E 511) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2019

items.title: E508 Potassium chloride
items.summary: Potassium chloride is a common replacer for sodium. EFSA found no safety concern at additive use, but extra potassium needs care for some people.
cautions: People with kidney disease, or on medicines that raise blood potassium, should ask a clinician before using potassium-based salt substitutes.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of hydrochloric acid (E 507), potassium chloride (E 508), calcium chloride (E 509) and magnesium chloride (E 511) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2019
US eCFR. 21 CFR 184.1622 Potassium chloride
US FDA. The Use of an Alternate Name for Potassium Chloride in Food Labeling
Clinical review of salt substitutes and hyperkalaemia, PMC

items.title: E509 Calcium chloride
items.summary: Calcium chloride keeps foods firm. EFSA saw no safety concern at current use.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of hydrochloric acid (E 507), potassium chloride (E 508), calcium chloride (E 509) and magnesium chloride (E 511) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2019
US eCFR. 21 CFR 184.1193 Calcium chloride

items.title: E511 Magnesium chloride
items.summary: Magnesium chloride is used to set tofu and firm foods. EFSA saw no safety concern at current use.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of hydrochloric acid (E 507), potassium chloride (E 508), calcium chloride (E 509) and magnesium chloride (E 511) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2019
US eCFR. 21 CFR 184.1426 Magnesium chloride

items.title: E513 Sulfuric acid
items.summary: EFSA re-evaluated sulphuric acid and its salts in 2019 and found no safety concern at current uses. We found no credible signal in recent human studies.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of sulphuric acid and its sodium, potassium, calcium and ammonium salts (E 513, 514, 515, 516 and 517) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2019

items.title: E514 Sodium sulfates
items.summary: EFSA re-evaluated sulphuric acid and its salts in 2019 and found no safety concern at current uses. We found no credible signal in recent human studies.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of sulphuric acid and its sodium, potassium, calcium and ammonium salts (E 513, 514, 515, 516 and 517) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2019

items.title: E516 Calcium sulfate
items.summary: Calcium sulfate is a mineral salt used in tofu and baking. EFSA saw no safety concern.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of sulphuric acid and its sodium, potassium, calcium and ammonium salts (E 513, 514, 515, 516, 517) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2019

items.title: E524 Sodium hydroxide
items.summary: Used in small amounts to adjust acidity or to process foods, and it reacts during processing. We found no credible safety signal for food use, though we did not find a recent EFSA opinion for it.
sources: EFSA. Call for data for the re-evaluation of food additives (EU programme under Regulation 257/2010), 2012

items.title: E529 Calcium oxide
items.summary: Calcium oxide is lime, used to adjust acidity during processing. We could not confirm a recent EFSA opinion.
sources: IPCS INCHEM. JECFA evaluation: calcium hydroxide and calcium oxide
EU. Commission Directive 2009/10/EC

items.title: E535 Sodium ferrocyanide
items.summary: Ferrocyanides are used mainly as anti-caking agents in salt. EFSA set a low group ADI and found current intake well below it.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of sodium ferrocyanide (E 535), potassium ferrocyanide (E 536) and calcium ferrocyanide (E 538) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2018
EFSA Journal 2018;16(7):5374

items.title: E536 Potassium ferrocyanide
items.summary: Ferrocyanides are used mainly as anti-caking agents in salt. EFSA set a low group ADI and found current intake well below it.

items.title: E551 Silicon dioxide
items.summary: EFSA found no safety concern at current uses in 2018 and again in 2024. It did note uncertainty about very small (nano) particles because long-term studies are lacking.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of silicon dioxide (E 551) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2018
EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of silicon dioxide (E 551) as a food additive in foods for infants below 16 weeks and follow-up for all population groups. EFSA Journal, 2024

items.title: E552 Calcium silicate
items.summary: In 2018 EFSA said it could not assess the safety of calcium silicate and related silicates because key data were missing. This is a data gap, not a finding of harm.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of calcium silicate (E 552), magnesium silicate (E 553a) and talc (E 553b) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2018
EFSA. Call for data for Talc E 553b

items.title: E553b Talc
items.summary: EFSA said in 2018 that it could not assess talc's safety as a food additive. IARC rated talc as probably carcinogenic to humans in 2025, based mainly on other kinds of exposure than eating.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of calcium silicate (E 552), magnesium silicate (E 553a) and talc (E 553b) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2018
EFSA. Call for data for Talc E 553b
IARC Monographs Volume 136: Talc and acrylonitrile, 2025

items.title: E554 Sodium aluminium silicate
items.summary: In 2020 EFSA said it could not assess the safety of this additive and flagged aluminium exposure from food supplements. This is a gap in data, not proof of harm.
cautions: People who use food supplements containing E 554 may go above the aluminium weekly limit, according to EFSA's estimate.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of sodium aluminium silicate (E 554) and potassium aluminium silicate (E 555) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2020

items.title: E555 Potassium aluminium silicate
items.summary: In 2020 EFSA said it could not assess the safety of this additive and flagged aluminium exposure from food supplements. This is a gap in data, not proof of harm.
cautions: People who use food supplements containing E 554 may go above the aluminium weekly limit, according to EFSA's estimate.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of sodium aluminium silicate (E 554) and potassium aluminium silicate (E 555) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2020

items.title: E559 Aluminium silicate
items.summary: A natural clay. We did not find a dedicated EFSA re-evaluation. It is a source of aluminium, for which EFSA set a weekly limit.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of sodium aluminium silicate (E 554) and potassium aluminium silicate (E 555) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2020
IPCS INCHEM. JECFA evaluation of aluminium silicate

items.title: E570 Fatty acids
items.summary: These are the same fatty acids found in ordinary fats and oils. EFSA found no safety concern in 2017, but noted limited long-term data.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of fatty acids (E 570) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2017

items.title: E574 Gluconic acid
items.summary: A mild acid that the body handles like a sugar-derived acid. EFSA has not yet finished its re-evaluation, and we found no credible signal.
sources: EFSA. Call for data for the re-evaluation of gluconic acid (E 574) and related food additives (E 575-579)

items.title: E575 Glucono delta-lactone
items.summary: A mild acid that the body handles like a sugar-derived acid. EFSA has not yet finished its re-evaluation, and we found no credible signal.

items.title: E620 Glutamic acid
items.summary: EFSA set a group safe daily intake for added glutamates in 2017 and found that some people, notably toddlers and children and high consumers, may go above it. Evidence for harm at normal food levels is weak.
cautions: Toddlers, children and people who eat a lot of savoury processed foods were the groups where EFSA estimated intake could exceed the safe level. Some people report short-lived symptoms such as headache after large doses of MSG, but blinded trials are mixed.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of glutamic acid (E 620), sodium glutamate (E 621), potassium glutamate (E 622), calcium glutamate (E 623), ammonium glutamate (E 624) and magnesium glutamate (E 625) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2017

items.title: E640 Glycine and its sodium salt
items.summary: Glycine is a common amino acid found in protein. We could not find a modern EFSA re-evaluation, so the safety picture rests on old assessments.
sources: Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/649 (amending EU additive specifications; lists E 640)
CSPI. Food additives: the definitive glossary (Chemical Cuisine)

items.title: E900 Dimethyl polysiloxane
items.summary: EFSA re-evaluated it in 2020 and set a safe daily intake with estimated exposure well below it.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of dimethyl polysiloxane (E 900) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2020

items.title: E901 Beeswax
items.summary: A natural wax made by bees. EFSA confirmed its safety in 2007 and JECFA found no concern at expected intake.
sources: EFSA AFC Panel. Beeswax (E 901) as a glazing agent and as carrier for flavours. EFSA Journal, 2007
JECFA. Beeswax evaluation (INCHEM)

items.title: E903 Carnauba wax
items.summary: A plant wax from palm leaves. EFSA found no safety concern at current use in 2012, though long-term studies are missing.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Scientific Opinion on the re-evaluation of carnauba wax (E 903) as a food additive. EFSA Journal, 2012

items.title: E904 Shellac
items.summary: A resin made by lac insects, so it is not vegetarian or vegan. EFSA set a safe daily intake in 2024, with a temporary limit for bleached types because of unknown impurities.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of shellac (E 904) as a food additive and a new application on the extension of use in dietary foods for special medical purposes. EFSA Journal, 2024
Same opinion, open-access text (PMC)

items.title: E920 L-cysteine
items.summary: An amino acid used to soften dough. We could not find a modern EFSA re-evaluation, so the evidence is thin rather than clear.
sources: Estonian Agriculture and Food Board. Additives authorised in flours (lists L-cysteine E 920)

items.title: E924 Potassium bromate
items.summary: IARC classes potassium bromate as possibly cancer-causing to humans (Group 2B) based on kidney and thyroid tumours in rats. It is banned in the EU and several other countries, but not banned federally in the US.
sources: CSPI. Food additives: the definitive glossary (Chemical Cuisine)

items.title: E927b Carbamide
items.summary: Urea is a normal body waste product. In the EU it is allowed only in sugar-free chewing gum. We could not find a modern EFSA re-evaluation.
sources: JECFA/FAO. Urea (Additive 485) specifications monograph

items.title: E941 Nitrogen
items.summary: Nitrogen is the main gas in air and is used to keep food fresh. We found no safety concern.
sources: EFSA. Call for data for the re-evaluation of food additives in gaseous form
EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of argon (E 938) and helium (E 939) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2024
US eCFR. 21 CFR Part 184 Subpart B, GRAS substances (includes 184.1540 nitrogen)

items.title: E943a Butane
items.summary: EFSA's 2025 re-evaluation found no safety concern at current uses. The only caveat is unclear impurity data.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of butane (E 943a), isobutane (E 943b) and propane (E 944) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2025

items.title: E943b Isobutane
items.summary: EFSA's 2025 re-evaluation found no safety concern at current uses. The only caveat is unclear impurity data.

items.title: E948 Oxygen

sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of oxygen (E 948) and hydrogen (E 949) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2025

items.title: E949 Hydrogen
items.summary: EFSA's 2025 re-evaluation found no safety concern and very low dietary exposure.
sources: EFSA FAF Panel. Re-evaluation of oxygen (E 948) and hydrogen (E 949) as food additives. EFSA Journal, 2025

items.title: E950 Acesulfame K
items.summary: EFSA raised its safe daily limit in 2025 and found no safety concern. One large French cohort linked higher intake to slightly more cancer, which does not prove cause.

items.title: E951 Aspartame
items.summary: IARC classed it as possibly carcinogenic in 2023 on limited evidence, while JECFA and EFSA kept the safe daily limit at 40 mg per kg.
cautions: People with phenylketonuria (PKU) must avoid it. EU and US labels say it contains a source of phenylalanine.
sources: IARC/WHO. Aspartame hazard and risk assessment results released by IARC and JECFA (press release). 2023
IARC/JECFA. Summary of findings: aspartame. WHO, 2023

items.title: E952 Cyclamic acid
items.summary: Banned in US food since 1969-70 after rat studies raised a cancer concern that later work did not firmly confirm. It is still allowed in the EU, where EFSA's re-evaluation is pending.
sources: Scientific Committee on Food. Opinion on cyclamic acid and its sodium and calcium salts. European Commission, 2000
EFSA. Update on the re-evaluation of sweeteners (Annex II, FAF plenary). July 2026
WHO/PAHO. WHO advises not to use non-sugar sweeteners for weight control in newly released guideline. 2023

items.title: E953 Isomalt
items.summary: No safety concern at normal use, but high intake can cause gas and loose stools.
cautions: People with irritable bowel syndrome or sensitive digestion.
sources: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2021/1175 (polyol labelling recital)
EFSA. Call for data on sweeteners authorised as food additives (polyols included)

items.title: E954 Saccharin
items.summary: EFSA raised the safe daily limit in 2024. Old rat bladder tumours are not thought to apply to people, but a small trial found effects on blood sugar.

items.title: E959 Neohesperidine DC

items.title: E961 Neotame

sources: EFSA. Update on the re-evaluation of sweeteners (Annex II, FAF plenary). July 2026
WHO/PAHO. WHO advises not to use non-sugar sweeteners for weight control in newly released guideline. 2023

items.title: E966 Lactitol
