WHO/PAHO. WHO advises not to use non-sugar sweeteners for weight control in newly released guideline. 2023

items.title: E999 Quillaia extract
items.summary: Quillaia extract is a foaming agent from tree bark. EFSA set an ADI in 2019 and later warned that wider use could exceed it.
sources: EFSA ANS Panel. Re-evaluation of quillaia extract (E 999) as a food additive and safety of the proposed extension of use. EFSA Journal, 2019
EFSA FAF Panel. Follow-up of the re-evaluation of quillaia extract (E 999) and safety of the proposed extension of uses. EFSA Journal, 2024

items.title: Ingredient Artificial flavouring
items.summary: Synthetic flavour molecules, each authorised on its own. The label doesn't say which ones are used.
sources: EU Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008 on flavourings (definitions, natural flavouring rules)

items.title: Ingredient Natural flavouring
items.summary: The label doesn't say what the flavour is made of. "Natural" describes where it came from or how it was made, not that it is simpler or safer.
sources: EU Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008 on flavourings (definitions, natural flavouring rules)

items.title: Ingredient Partially hydrogenated oil
items.summary: Partially hydrogenated oils are the main source of industrial trans fat, which raises heart disease risk. The US has removed their GRAS status, and the EU caps trans fat.
sources: FDA: Final determination regarding partially hydrogenated oils (removing trans fat)
Federal Register: Final determination regarding partially hydrogenated oils, 17 June 2015
EU Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/649 on trans fat other than trans fat naturally occurring in fat of animal origin

items.title: Ingredient Hydrolysed protein
items.summary: Protein broken into amino acids to add savoury taste. Acid-hydrolysed types can contain a process contaminant called 3-MCPD.
cautions: People with a soy, wheat or milk allergy, depending on the source.
sources: EFSA: 3-MCPD in food, tolerable intake set in 2018

items.title: Ingredient Maltodextrin
items.summary: A quickly digested starch product. Lab and mouse studies suggest it may favour some gut bacteria linked to Crohn's disease. This hasn't been shown in people.
sources: Nickerson KP, McDonald C. Crohn's disease-associated adherent-invasive E. coli adhesion is enhanced by exposure to the dietary polysaccharide maltodextrin. PLoS ONE, 2012

items.title: Ingredient Vanillin
items.summary: The main flavour compound of vanilla. Most vanillin in food is made from other sources. Regulators allow it as a flavour.
sources: FEMA Flavor Library: Vanillin (industry flavour association)
US Code of Federal Regulations 21 CFR 182.60: synthetic flavoring substances and adjuvants

items.title: Ingredient Yeast extract
items.summary: A food ingredient, not an E-number. It contains natural free glutamate, which gives savoury taste, as added MSG does.
sources: EFSA: Re-evaluation of glutamic acid and glutamates (E 620-625), 2017

items.title: 4-7-8 breathing
items.summary: 4 in · 7 hold · 8 out. In bed, to help you drift off. Popularized by Dr. Andrew Weil.
items.why: A very long exhale with a hold slows breathing to about three breaths a minute. Small studies show short-term drops in heart rate and blood pressure. It may feel light-headed at first; start with four cycles.

items.title: Alternate nostril breathing
items.summary: Left in · right out · right in · left out. A steadying practice for a busy mind. Rest your right hand on your face and close one nostril at a time.
items.why: A 2024 analysis of six trials with 525 people found it lowered blood pressure more than no intervention. But the trials were small, often unblinded, and varied a lot, so the result should be read with care. Evidence for stress and anxiety specifically is thinner.

items.title: Belly breathing
items.summary: 4 in · 6 out, low and slow. When your shoulders are tight and your breath feels high in your chest. Good for learning to breathe from the diaphragm.
items.why: Slow breathing from the diaphragm slows breathing rate, pulse and blood pressure. A systematic review of it as a stand-alone stress practice found only a few well-run studies, so the evidence is encouraging but not strong. It's a good base for every other technique.

items.title: Box breathing
items.summary: 4 · 4 · 4 · 4. Before a big moment: a meeting, a game, a hard conversation.
items.why: Used by military and first responders to stay steady under pressure. In the same Stanford trial, box breathing improved mood too, a little less than cyclic sighing. Research on it alone is limited.

items.title: Settle in
items.summary: 4 in · 6 out. Any time you feel wound up. A gentle place to begin.
items.why: Breathing out for longer than you breathe in, at around six breaths a minute, shifts your body toward its relaxed, rest-and-digest mode. Slow-paced breathing reliably raises heart rate variability, a marker of that shift.

items.title: Coherent breathing
items.summary: 5.5 in · 5.5 out. A steady 10-minute practice for everyday resilience.
items.why: About five and a half breaths a minute lines your breathing up with your heart's natural rhythm (resonance). A meta-analysis of 58 studies found practicing this pace improves anxiety, stress and mood.

items.title: Humming breath
items.summary: 4 in · 8 hum out. When you want something to focus on. The soft hum gives your attention an anchor, and it's discreet enough for a quiet room.
items.why: Studies of humming breath (bhramari) are small and mostly without control groups. They report better heart rate variability and lower anxiety scores, but the long, slow out-breath is probably doing much of the work, as in other slow-breathing practices. Treat it as a pleasant, low-risk option rather than a proven one.

items.title: Power breathing
items.summary: Rounds of deep breaths and holds. Morning energy. Inspired by the Wim Hof style. Sit or lie down.
items.why: Fast, deep breathing followed by a breath hold. In the Stanford trial it raised energy and mood. A well-known 2014 study found trained practitioners had a dampened immune response to a bacterial toxin. It's powerful, and it can make you faint.
cautions: Has a safety check before it starts. Sit or lie down.

items.title: Physiological sigh
items.summary: In, top up, long out. The fastest reset when stress spikes. Even one or two help.
items.why: In a Stanford trial of 111 people, five minutes a day of cyclic sighing for a month improved mood and lowered breathing rate more than mindfulness meditation did. The double inhale re-opens tiny air sacs in the lungs; the long exhale slows the heart.

items.title: Triangle breathing
items.summary: 4 in · 4 hold · 4 out. A simple pattern for racing thoughts, when box breathing feels like one step too many.
items.why: A three-part rhythm gives your mind something simple to follow, and slow, even breathing is what most of the research on breathing and stress supports. There's no research on this exact pattern, so we rate it as early evidence.

items.title: Evening Reset
items.summary: From wired to winding down. Best in the evening.
items.why: Each piece has its own evidence: dim light and no screens before bed, slow breathing, muscle relaxation, and a relaxing sound. Together they give your body a clear signal that the day is over.

items.title: Focus Launch
items.summary: Clear the decks, then go deep. Best any time.
items.why: Removing your phone from sight reduces distraction, and a short breathing practice settles you before you start. The evidence for binaural beats and focus is mixed, so treat the session as a pleasant, consistent start signal.

items.title: Gratitude Minute
items.summary: Write it down, breathe it in. Best any time.
items.why: Regularly writing down things you're grateful for is linked with better mood in many studies, though effects are modest. Pairing it with slow breathing makes it a relaxed minute either way.

items.title: Midday Reset
items.summary: Undo the morning slump. Best in the midday.
items.why: Breaking up sitting, light walking after a meal, and a glass of water are simple, well-supported ways to steady energy and blood sugar in the afternoon.

items.title: Morning Armor
items.summary: Light, water, breath, go. Best in the morning.
items.why: Morning daylight sets your body clock and helps you feel alert, water replaces what you lost overnight, and a few minutes of breathing and movement wake up your body before the day starts pulling at you.

items.title: Gentle Reset
items.summary: Three minutes back to ease. Best any time.
items.why: Cyclic sighing is one of the fastest ways to lower arousal, grounding pulls your attention out of the spiral and into the room, and slow breathing keeps you there.

items.title: Sunday Restore
items.summary: A slower reset for the week ahead. Best any time.
items.why: Gentle yoga eases stiffness and stress, a moment of reflection helps you choose what matters, and reaching out to someone is one of the most reliable mood boosters there is.

items.title: Apple cider vinegar
items.summary: Great in dressings. The health claims are mostly small studies.
items.why: Small studies show vinegar with a meal can slightly blunt the blood sugar rise afterwards. Weight-loss and 'detox' claims aren't well supported.
cautions: Undiluted vinegar can burn your throat and wear away tooth enamel.
Can lower potassium, especially with diuretics or insulin.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Almonds
items.summary: Protein, fiber, vitamin E and magnesium in one handful.
items.why: Part of the nut mix in PREDIMED. A good source of vitamin E and magnesium.
cautions: Tree nut allergy.

items.title: Ashwagandha
items.summary: An Ayurvedic root sold mostly as a supplement for stress and sleep.
items.why: Some small, short trials suggest it may reduce stress and improve sleep. Longer, larger studies are lacking (NCCIH).
cautions: Linked to rare cases of liver injury (NCCIH).
Avoid in pregnancy. May affect thyroid hormone levels and interact with sedatives and immune-suppressing medicine.
Sold as a supplement, which the FDA doesn't check for purity or strength before sale. If you buy one, look for a USP or NSF seal.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Avocado
items.summary: Creamy, filling, and full of fiber and unsaturated fat.
items.why: About 10 grams of fiber per avocado (USDA). Swapping saturated fats for unsaturated fats like these lowers LDL cholesterol.
cautions: Calorie-dense; enjoy it in place of other fats, not on top of them.

items.title: Barley
items.summary: A chewy whole grain with the same cholesterol-lowering fiber as oats.
items.why: Covered by the same FDA beta-glucan health claim as oats. A whole grain high in fiber.
cautions: Contains gluten.

items.title: Beets
items.summary: Sweet, earthy and one of the richest food sources of nitrate.
items.why: Beetroot juice modestly lowers blood pressure in trials (meta-analysis). Studied for exercise endurance, with some positive results.
cautions: Can turn urine pink. It's harmless.
High in oxalate if you're prone to kidney stones.

items.title: Black beans
items.summary: Fiber-rich, satisfying, and cheap.
items.why: Pulses lower LDL cholesterol in trials. About 15 grams of fiber per cooked cup (USDA).
cautions: Rinse canned beans to reduce sodium.

items.title: Blueberries
items.summary: Fiber and anthocyanins. Frozen counts.
items.why: Higher berry and flavonoid intake is linked with lower type 2 diabetes and heart risk in large observational studies. A good source of fiber and vitamin C.
cautions: None for most people.

items.title: Broccoli
items.summary: A cruciferous vegetable with fiber, vitamin C and sulforaphane.
items.why: Cruciferous vegetables are linked to lower risk of some diseases in observational studies. Very high in vitamin C and fiber.
cautions: Can cause gas as you increase fiber. Build up slowly.

items.title: Burdock root
items.summary: A long, earthy root eaten as a vegetable in Japan and used in herbal traditions worldwide.
items.why: Rich in inulin, a prebiotic fiber that feeds gut bacteria, like other fiber-rich foods. Lab and animal studies show antioxidant compounds, but there are very few studies in people. Claims that it 'purifies the blood' or detoxes the body aren't backed by human research. Your liver and kidneys do that job.
cautions: Buy it, don't forage it. Wild burdock root can be confused with toxic plants like belladonna.
May lower blood sugar. If you take diabetes medicine, watch your levels.
Avoid if you're allergic to ragweed, daisies or chrysanthemums (same plant family).
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Chamomile tea
items.summary: The classic bedtime tea. A warm, caffeine-free ritual with modest evidence.
items.why: Small studies on sleep and anxiety show modest or mixed results (NCCIH). A warm caffeine-free drink is a good wind-down cue in itself.
cautions: Avoid if you're allergic to ragweed or daisies.
May interact with some medicines, including warfarin and cyclosporine.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Chia seeds
items.summary: Tiny seeds with a big dose of fiber.
items.why: About 10 grams of fiber per ounce (USDA). Contain ALA, a plant omega-3.
cautions: Always soak chia or eat it with plenty of liquid. Dry seeds swell and have caused choking.
Increase slowly as with any high-fiber food.

items.title: Chickpeas
items.summary: The base of hummus, falafel and countless stews.
items.why: Pulses lower LDL cholesterol in trials. High in fiber, protein and folate.
cautions: Rinse canned chickpeas to reduce sodium.

items.title: Cinnamon (Ceylon)
items.summary: A warm spice studied for blood sugar, with inconsistent results.
items.why: Studies on blood sugar in type 2 diabetes conflict. It isn't a substitute for treatment (NCCIH). A good way to add sweetness and flavor without adding sugar.
cautions: Common cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which in large amounts can harm the liver. Ceylon cinnamon has far less. Sprinkling it on food is fine; heaping spoonfuls every day aren't.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Dandelion greens
items.summary: A bitter leafy green, rich in vitamins A and K.
items.why: Very nutrient-dense: lots of vitamin K and vitamin A, plus fiber (USDA). One small human study suggested a mild diuretic effect. That's all the human evidence there is.
cautions: Large amounts of vitamin K can change how warfarin works. If you take it, keep your intake steady and tell your clinician.
If you forage, avoid lawns, roadsides and anywhere that might be sprayed.
Avoid if you're allergic to ragweed or daisies.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Dark chocolate (70%+)
items.summary: A treat with interesting, but mixed, heart research.
items.why: In the COSMOS trial, cocoa flavanol supplements didn't significantly reduce overall heart events, though deaths from heart disease were lower. Chocolate bars contain far less flavanol, plus sugar.
cautions: Some dark chocolate bars have tested high for lead and cadmium. Vary brands and keep portions small.

items.title: Elderberry
items.summary: Dark purple berries made into syrups, popular for colds and flu.
items.why: A few small studies suggest it may shorten flu or cold symptoms, but the evidence is limited (NCCIH).
cautions: Raw berries, leaves and stems can cause nausea and vomiting. Always cook elderberries.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Epsom salt
items.summary: A bath soak. The warm bath helps; magnesium through the skin isn't proven.
items.why: There's no good evidence that your skin absorbs meaningful magnesium from a bath (Nutrients, 2017 review). A warm bath 1 to 2 hours before bed can help you fall asleep, salt or no salt.
cautions: If you have diabetes or nerve damage in your feet, ask before long foot soaks.
Avoid on broken skin.

items.title: Extra virgin olive oil
items.summary: The backbone of the Mediterranean diet, backed by a large trial.
items.why: In PREDIMED, a Mediterranean diet with about 4 tablespoons a day of extra virgin olive oil cut major heart events by about 30% versus a low-fat diet.
cautions: Calorie-dense. Use it in place of butter and other fats.

items.title: Ground flaxseed
items.summary: Fiber and omega-3, with a trial showing lower blood pressure.
items.why: In a six-month trial, 30 g of ground flaxseed a day lowered blood pressure in people with peripheral artery disease. Rich in fiber and ALA.
cautions: Drink water with it.
May affect blood sugar and blood thinners in large amounts.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Garlic
items.summary: A kitchen essential with small, real effects on blood pressure and cholesterol in some studies.
items.why: Some studies find small drops in blood pressure and cholesterol, but results vary (NCCIH). There's no good evidence that garlic prevents colds.
cautions: Garlic supplements can increase bleeding risk with blood thinners and before surgery.
Can cause heartburn and, well, garlic breath.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Ginger
items.summary: A spicy root with the best evidence of any kitchen herb, for nausea.
items.why: May ease nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, according to NCCIH's review of trials. Studied for nausea after surgery and during chemotherapy, with mixed results. Small trials on arthritis pain and menstrual cramps are promising but not conclusive.
cautions: Can cause heartburn or stomach upset in large amounts.
Talk to your clinician before using ginger for nausea in pregnancy.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Green tea
items.summary: A gentler caffeine source, with L-theanine for a gentler lift.
items.why: Has about a third to half the caffeine of coffee, plus L-theanine, which may smooth the jitters. Observational studies link it to better heart health, but trials haven't proven it prevents disease (NCCIH).
cautions: Concentrated green tea extract supplements have been linked to liver injury. The tea itself hasn't.
Counts toward your daily caffeine (FDA suggests up to 400 mg a day for most adults).
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Hibiscus tea
items.summary: Tart, ruby-red and caffeine-free. Small trials suggest a modest effect on blood pressure.
items.why: Several small trials found modest drops in blood pressure in people with mildly high blood pressure. It isn't a substitute for medicine.
cautions: May add to the effect of blood pressure medicine.
Avoid in pregnancy.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Kefir
items.summary: A drinkable fermented milk with many strains of microbes.
items.why: Part of the fermented-food diet that raised microbiome diversity in the 2021 Stanford trial. Usually well tolerated by people with lactose intolerance.
cautions: Choose plain to avoid added sugar.

items.title: Kimchi
items.summary: Spicy fermented cabbage, a Korean staple.
items.why: A fermented food with live microbes; part of the 2021 Stanford trial diet. Research on specific health effects is early.
cautions: High in sodium. A little goes a long way if you watch salt.

items.title: Kombucha
items.summary: Fizzy fermented tea. Popular, with almost no human research.
items.why: A lower-sugar alternative to soda. Health claims are based mainly on lab and animal studies.
cautions: Contains a little alcohol and caffeine.
Home brewing can grow harmful microbes; follow tested methods.
Not recommended in pregnancy or for people with weakened immune systems.

items.title: Kale and collards
items.summary: Dark leafy greens: fiber, folate, vitamin K and nitrate.
items.why: Dietary nitrate from leafy greens and beets modestly lowers blood pressure in trials. Higher vegetable intake is linked with lower heart disease risk in large cohorts.
cautions: Large amounts of vitamin K can change how warfarin works. If you take it, keep your intake steady and tell your clinician.

items.title: Lemon balm tea
items.summary: A lemony mint-family herb, used for relaxation and sleep.
items.why: A few small trials suggest relaxing effects, often in blends with valerian. Better studies are needed.
cautions: May add to the effect of sedatives and thyroid medicine.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Lentils
items.summary: Fast-cooking, cheap, and packed with protein and fiber.
items.why: About one serving of beans, peas or lentils a day lowered LDL cholesterol in a meta-analysis of trials. Legumes are a daily staple in every Blue Zone.
cautions: Increase slowly if you're not used to fiber, and drink water with it.

items.title: Miso
items.summary: Fermented soybean paste that adds deep savory flavor.
items.why: A fermented food, but cooking or boiling it kills the live microbes. Adds savory depth with a small amount.
cautions: Very high in sodium.

items.title: Moringa leaf
items.summary: A nutrient-dense leaf from a fast-growing tropical tree, usually sold as a powder.
items.why: The leaves are rich in vitamins and minerals. Human trials for blood sugar and other claims are small and early.
cautions: Avoid the root and bark, especially in pregnancy.
May lower blood sugar and blood pressure.
Sold as a supplement, which the FDA doesn't check for purity or strength before sale. If you buy one, look for a USP or NSF seal.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Stinging nettle
items.summary: A wild green that loses its sting when cooked. Tastes like earthy spinach.
items.why: Nutritious as a cooked green. Studied for hay fever and enlarged prostate, with small and mixed results.
cautions: Raw leaves sting. Wear gloves when handling.
May affect blood pressure, blood sugar and diuretic medicines.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Oats
items.summary: One of the few foods with an FDA-authorized heart health claim.
items.why: Beta-glucan, the soluble fiber in oats, lowers LDL cholesterol. The FDA allows a heart-health claim at 3 g of beta-glucan a day (about 1.5 cups of cooked oatmeal). High-fiber diets (25 to 29 g a day) are linked to 15 to 30% lower risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer (Lancet, 2019).
cautions: If you have celiac disease, buy oats labelled gluten-free.

items.title: Peppermint tea
items.summary: Refreshing and caffeine-free. Peppermint oil capsules have real evidence for IBS.
items.why: Enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules may ease irritable bowel syndrome symptoms (NCCIH). The tea is much weaker, but many people find it soothing after meals.
cautions: Can worsen heartburn and acid reflux.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Pumpkin seeds
items.summary: One of the richest food sources of magnesium.
items.why: About 150 mg of magnesium per ounce, more than a third of the daily need for most adults (NIH). Food sources of magnesium have no upper limit; the 350 mg limit applies only to supplements.
cautions: None for most people.

items.title: Quinoa
items.summary: A quick-cooking whole grain with complete protein.
items.why: Contains all essential amino acids, plus fiber and magnesium. Whole grains in place of refined grains are linked to lower disease risk.
cautions: Rinse it to remove its bitter coating (saponins).

items.title: Raw honey
items.summary: A sweetener with a real use: soothing coughs in children over one.
items.why: A Cochrane review found honey may ease cough symptoms in children better than no treatment.
cautions: Never give honey to babies under 12 months. It can cause infant botulism.
It's still sugar, so be mindful if you're managing blood sugar.

items.title: Rooibos tea
items.summary: A naturally caffeine-free red tea from South Africa. Good for evenings.
items.why: Caffeine-free and low in tannins. Antioxidant claims come mostly from lab studies; human research is limited.
cautions: Generally considered safe as a drink.

items.title: Salmon
items.summary: Omega-3 rich fish. The American Heart Association recommends two servings of fish a week.
items.why: Eating fish once or twice a week is linked to lower risk of heart disease death (AHA science advisory). Rich in EPA and DHA omega-3s, protein and vitamin D.
cautions: Salmon is low in mercury and on the FDA's 'best choices' list.

items.title: Sardines
items.summary: Small, cheap, low in mercury, and loaded with omega-3s and calcium.
items.why: Among the richest sources of omega-3s. Eaten with their soft bones, they're a good calcium source.
cautions: Low in mercury (FDA 'best choices'). Canned can be salty; check labels.

items.title: Sauerkraut
items.summary: Fermented cabbage. Only the refrigerated kind has live cultures.
items.why: A fermented food with live microbes, when unpasteurized. Easy to make at home with cabbage and salt.
cautions: High in sodium.
Shelf-stable jars are pasteurized, so the microbes are gone.

items.title: Sea moss
items.summary: A red seaweed that's popular online, with very little research in people.
items.why: Contains some minerals and fiber like other seaweeds. Popular claims about '92 minerals', immunity and thyroid health have little human research behind them.
cautions: Iodine content varies a lot and can be very high, which can upset your thyroid.
Seaweed can carry heavy metals. Buy brands that publish lab testing.
Ask your clinician first if you have a thyroid condition.

items.title: Shiitake mushrooms
items.summary: Savory, meaty mushrooms with a small amount of immune research.
items.why: One small trial found changes in immune markers after daily shiitake. It's early research. Adds deep savory flavor, so you need less salt.
cautions: Cook them well. Raw or undercooked shiitake can cause an itchy, streaky rash in some people.

items.title: Spinach
items.summary: An easy green that disappears into almost anything.
items.why: A source of folate, vitamin K, magnesium and nitrate. Nitrate-rich vegetables modestly lower blood pressure.
cautions: High in oxalate. If you've had calcium-oxalate kidney stones, ask about portion sizes.
Large amounts of vitamin K can change how warfarin works. If you take it, keep your intake steady and tell your clinician.

items.title: Sweet potato
items.summary: Fiber, potassium and lots of beta-carotene.
items.why: One medium sweet potato covers more than a day's vitamin A, as beta-carotene (USDA). Fiber-rich whole foods are linked to lower disease risk.
cautions: None for most people.

items.title: Holy basil
items.summary: A fragrant basil sacred in Hinduism, now popular as a relaxing tea.
items.why: A few small trials suggest it may help with stress, but they're small and short. A pleasant, caffeine-free tea.
cautions: Avoid in pregnancy or if trying to conceive; animal studies raise questions.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Turmeric
items.summary: The golden spice in curry. Hugely popular, though the research is weaker than the hype.
items.why: Curcumin, its main compound, is studied for joint pain and inflammation, with mixed and mostly small trials. Curcumin is poorly absorbed on its own. Black pepper and fat increase absorption. As a spice in food, it's safe and flavorful. The case for high-dose supplements isn't settled.
cautions: Turmeric supplements have been linked to rare cases of liver injury (NCCIH). This hasn't been seen with turmeric in food.
Supplements may interact with blood thinners and diabetes medicine.
Sold as a supplement, which the FDA doesn't check for purity or strength before sale. If you buy one, look for a USP or NSF seal.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Valerian root tea
items.summary: An old sleep remedy. Strong smell, mixed evidence.
items.why: Studies on sleep are inconsistent; some people report it helps them fall asleep (NCCIH).
cautions: Don't combine with alcohol, sleep aids or other sedatives, or drive after taking it.
Not recommended in pregnancy or for children under 3.
Pregnant, breastfeeding, on prescription medicine, or managing a health condition? Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it as a remedy.

items.title: Walnuts
items.summary: The nut highest in plant omega-3 (ALA).
items.why: In PREDIMED, a Mediterranean diet with a daily handful of mixed nuts (half walnuts) cut major heart events by about 30% versus a low-fat diet. Rich in ALA, a plant omega-3.
cautions: Tree nut allergy.

items.title: Plain yogurt
items.summary: Protein, calcium and live cultures.
items.why: In 2024 the FDA allowed a qualified claim that eating yogurt regularly may reduce type 2 diabetes risk (limited evidence). In a 10-week trial, a diet high in fermented foods increased gut microbiome diversity and lowered inflammation markers.
cautions: Choose plain; flavored yogurts can have as much sugar as dessert.
Look for 'live and active cultures' on the label.

items.title: Bedtime stretch
items.summary: Stretching, 5 min. In bed or on the floor, with the lights low.

items.title: Qigong: Eight Brocades, part one
items.summary: Qigong, 5 min. Morning energy without strain. The first four movements of Ba Duan Jin.

items.title: Desk reset
items.summary: Stretching, 3 min. Every hour or two of sitting. No need to stand up.

items.title: Tai chi basics
items.summary: Tai chi, 5 min. Standing, any time. Slow and smooth is the whole point.

items.title: Morning wake-up
items.summary: Stretching, 4 min. Right after you get up, ideally near a window.

items.title: After-meal walk
items.summary: Walking, 10 min. After your biggest meal. Even two minutes blunts the blood sugar spike.

items.title: Gentle yoga flow
items.summary: Yoga, 8 min. Morning or evening, on a mat or carpet. Beginner friendly.

items.title: Thiamin
items.summary: Helps turn food into energy and keeps nerves working. Found in: Sunflower seeds, Black beans, lentils, peas, Whole grains and brown rice, Fortified cereals and breads.
items.why: Helps cells turn carbohydrate into energy (strong evidence). Supports nerve and heart function. Severe lack causes beriberi.
cautions: Thiamin from food and standard supplements is very safe. A clinician should guide it if you drink heavily or have had weight-loss surgery.

items.title: Vitamin B12
items.summary: Keeps nerves and blood cells healthy. Found naturally only in animal foods. Found in: None naturally. Fortified nutritional yeast, plant milks and cereals, Some fortified meat substitutes.
items.why: Needed to make red blood cells and DNA, and to protect nerves (strong evidence). Low levels over time can cause anaemia and nerve damage.
cautions: Ask a clinician about a blood test if you fit the groups above, or have tingling hands and feet or unusual tiredness.
Check with a pharmacist if you take metformin or acid reducers.

items.title: Riboflavin
items.summary: Helps make energy and keeps skin and eyes healthy. Found in: Almonds, Mushrooms, Spinach, Fortified cereals.
items.why: Helps cells make energy from food (strong evidence). Supports skin, eyes and the nervous system. High-dose riboflavin has been studied for migraine prevention with some benefit in small trials (mixed evidence).
cautions: Safe from food. Ask a clinician before using high-dose supplements for migraines.

items.title: Niacin
items.summary: Helps cells release energy and make and repair DNA. Found in: Peanuts and peanut butter, Mushrooms, Brown rice and whole grains, Green peas.
items.why: Part of the machinery cells use to produce energy (strong evidence). Severe lack causes pellagra.
cautions: Supplement forms in higher amounts cause flushing, and in larger amounts can harm the liver. Doctors sometimes prescribe niacin for cholesterol, only with monitoring.

items.title: Pantothenic acid
items.summary: Helps your body use fats and carbohydrates for energy. Found in: Shiitake mushrooms, Avocado, Sweet potato, Sunflower seeds.
items.why: Part of coenzyme A, which is needed to make energy and many body compounds (strong evidence).
cautions: Very safe. Very high supplement amounts can cause digestive upset.

items.title: Vitamin B6
items.summary: Helps make brain chemicals and process protein. Found in: Chickpeas, Potatoes, Bananas, Fortified cereals.
items.why: Involved in more than 100 enzyme reactions, mostly in protein metabolism (strong evidence). Needed to make serotonin, dopamine and haemoglobin. Used in pregnancy for nausea under clinician advice (moderate evidence).
cautions: Taking too much from supplements for months can damage nerves, causing numbness and pain. Food is not a risk.
Check with a pharmacist if you take anti-seizure drugs.

items.title: Biotin
items.summary: Helps turn food into energy. Its famous hair and nail claims are not well supported. Found in: Sunflower seeds, Almonds and peanuts, Sweet potatoes, Spinach.
items.why: Helps enzymes break down fats, carbohydrates and protein (strong evidence it's needed). Biotin for hair, skin or nails in people who are not low: little good evidence (weak evidence).
cautions: Biotin supplements can distort common lab tests, including thyroid and heart-attack (troponin) blood tests. The US FDA warns about this. Tell any clinician or lab you take it, and stop it before tests if they advise.

items.title: Calcium
items.summary: The main mineral in bones and teeth, and a signal for muscles and nerves. Found in: Calcium-set tofu, Fortified plant milks and juices, Kale, bok choy, collard greens, Broccoli.
items.why: Builds and maintains bones and teeth (strong evidence). Needed for muscle contraction, nerve signals and blood clotting. Calcium supplements alone have only a small effect on fractures, and work best with enough vitamin D (moderate evidence).
cautions: Too much from supplements can cause constipation and kidney stones. Ask a clinician about supplements, especially if you've had stones.
Calcium can reduce how well some medicines work (certain antibiotics, thyroid medicine, iron). Space them apart and ask a pharmacist.

items.title: Choline
items.summary: Builds cell membranes and a brain chemical for memory and muscle control. Found in: Soybeans and tofu, Quinoa, Broccoli and Brussels sprouts, Potatoes.
items.why: Needed for cell membranes and for acetylcholine, a messenger for memory, mood and muscles (strong evidence). Important for a baby's brain development in pregnancy (moderate evidence).
cautions: Very high supplement amounts can cause a fishy body odour, low blood pressure and nausea. Food is fine.

items.title: Chromium
items.summary: A trace mineral often marketed for blood sugar. The evidence for that is thin. Found in: Broccoli, Whole grains, Potatoes, Grape juice.
items.why: May help insulin work, but whether people need more is unclear, and true deficiency is very rare (weak evidence). Chromium supplements for blood sugar or weight loss: results are mixed and small (mixed evidence).
cautions: If you have diabetes, ask your care team before taking chromium, since it may change how your medicines work.

items.title: Copper
items.summary: Helps use iron, build connective tissue and support nerves. Found in: Cashews, sunflower seeds, sesame seeds, Shiitake mushrooms, Chickpeas and lentils, Dark chocolate.
items.why: Needed to make energy, use iron and form connective tissue and blood vessels (strong evidence). Supports nerve and immune function.
cautions: Supplements are rarely needed. Too much can harm the liver. Ask a clinician, especially with liver disease.

items.title: Folate
items.summary: Builds DNA and red blood cells. Important before and during early pregnancy. Found in: Lentils, chickpeas, black beans, Spinach, kale, romaine, Asparagus and Brussels sprouts, Broccoli.
items.why: Needed to make DNA and new cells and to form red blood cells (strong evidence). Taking folic acid before and in early pregnancy lowers the chance of neural tube defects such as spina bifida (strong evidence).
cautions: If there is any chance of pregnancy, ask a clinician about folic acid. It matters before you know you are pregnant.
A lot of folic acid can hide the signs of low vitamin B12. Ask a clinician if you are over 50 or eat no animal foods.

items.title: Iodine
items.summary: The thyroid needs it to make hormones that set your metabolism. Found in: Seaweed (nori, kelp, wakame: amounts vary a lot), Iodised salt, Prunes and lima beans (small amounts).
items.why: Used to make thyroid hormones, which control metabolism, growth and a baby's brain development (strong evidence). Too little can cause goitre and, in pregnancy, harm brain development.
cautions: Kelp and some seaweed hold a very large and variable amount, and too much can cause thyroid problems just as too little can. Ask a clinician before kelp supplements, and if you have thyroid disease.

items.title: Iron
items.summary: Carries oxygen in your blood and to your muscles. Found in: Lentils, chickpeas, beans, Tofu and tempeh, Spinach and Swiss chard, Pumpkin and sesame seeds.
items.why: Makes haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells (strong evidence). Needed for energy, focus and immune function. Low iron can bring tiredness, breathlessness and pale skin.
cautions: Don't take iron supplements unless a blood test shows you need them. Extra iron can build up and cause harm, and it upsets the stomach.
People with hemochromatosis should avoid extra iron and vitamin C supplements.
Keep iron supplements away from children. An overdose can be dangerous.

items.title: Magnesium
items.summary: A helper in over 300 reactions: muscles, nerves, blood sugar, blood pressure and bones. Found in: Pumpkin seeds and chia seeds, Almonds, cashews, peanuts, Spinach and Swiss chard, Black beans, edamame, lentils.
items.why: Needed for hundreds of enzyme reactions, including making energy, muscle contraction and nerve signals (strong evidence it is essential). Higher intakes are linked to lower blood pressure, and supplements lower it modestly in some studies (moderate evidence). Helps turn vitamin D into its active form (moderate…
cautions: Supplement forms (not food) can cause diarrhoea and cramps in higher amounts.
Ask a clinician or pharmacist first if you have kidney disease, or take antibiotics (tetracyclines, quinolones), bisphosphonates, diuretics or long-term stomach-acid medicines. These can interact.

items.title: Manganese
items.summary: A helper for bone formation and for breaking down carbohydrates and cholesterol. Found in: Hazelnuts and pecans, Brown rice and oats, Chickpeas and lentils, Pineapple.
items.why: Part of enzymes involved in bone formation, metabolism and antioxidant defence (strong evidence it's needed). Shortage is very rare, so benefits from extra are unproven (weak evidence).
cautions: Too much can affect the nervous system. It is most often linked to heavy workplace exposure or some well water, rather than food. Avoid high-dose supplements.

items.title: Molybdenum
items.summary: A trace mineral for enzymes that break down toxins and process proteins. Found in: Legumes: lentils, black-eyed peas, beans, Whole grains, Nuts, Leafy vegetables.
items.why: Part of enzymes that process certain amino acids and clear waste (strong evidence it's needed). Deficiency has only been seen in rare inherited conditions or unusual tube feeding.
cautions: Supplements are not needed and very high amounts can cause problems. Skip them unless a clinician advises.

items.title: Phosphorus
items.summary: A partner of calcium in bones, and part of the molecule that carries energy. Found in: Lentils, chickpeas, beans, Nuts and seeds, Whole grains, oats, Potatoes.
items.why: Builds bones and teeth with calcium (strong evidence). Part of DNA and ATP, the cell's energy currency.
cautions: If you have kidney disease, you may need to limit phosphorus, including additives. Ask your care team.

items.title: Potassium
items.summary: Helps balance fluids, power muscles and nerves, and keeps blood pressure in range. Found in: Potatoes and sweet potatoes, Beans, lentils, white beans, Spinach and Swiss chard, Bananas, oranges, cantaloupe.
items.why: Balances fluids and supports nerve signals and muscle contraction, including the heart (strong evidence). Eating more potassium-rich foods, along with less sodium, lowers blood pressure (strong evidence, the basis of the DASH eating pattern). It may reduce the risk of kidney stones and bone loss (moderate evidence).
cautions: Ask a clinician before increasing potassium or using salt substitutes if you have kidney disease or take ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics. Too much can affect heart rhythm.
Most store-bought potassium supplements hold only a small amount, so food is the main route.

items.title: Selenium
items.summary: A tiny amount powers antioxidant enzymes and thyroid hormones. Found in: Brazil nuts (very high), Whole grains and brown rice, Sunflower seeds, Mushrooms.
items.why: Part of enzymes that protect cells and help the thyroid make and use hormones (strong evidence). Selenium supplements have not been shown to prevent cancer or heart disease in people who aren't low (moderate evidence of no benefit).
cautions: Too much is harmful: hair and nail loss, nerve problems. Avoid high-dose supplements and eating Brazil nuts by the handful every day.

items.title: Vitamin A
items.summary: For vision, immune defences, skin and growth. Found in: Sweet potato, Carrots, Spinach, kale, collards, Butternut squash and pumpkin.
items.why: Makes the pigment your eyes use in dim light; lack is a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide (strong evidence). Supports the immune system and the lining of your skin, gut and lungs. Needed for growth and development before birth.
cautions: Ready-made vitamin A (retinol) from liver, cod liver oil or supplements is harmful in high amounts, and excess in pregnancy is linked to birth defects. Talk to a clinician if you are or may become pregnant.
Beta-carotene supplements raised lung cancer risk in people who smoke. Food sources are fine.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.summary: Builds collagen, supports immunity and helps you take up iron from plants. Found in: Red and yellow peppers, Oranges, grapefruit, kiwi, strawberries, Broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, Tomatoes, potatoes.
items.why: Needed to make collagen for skin, blood vessels, bones and wound healing; severe lack causes scurvy (strong evidence). Helps your body absorb iron from plant foods (strong evidence). Acts as an antioxidant. Regular extra doses may slightly shorten colds, but they don't stop them (moderate evidence).
cautions: Very large supplement amounts can cause stomach upset and kidney stones in some people.
Ask a clinician if you have had kidney stones or have a condition that stores too much iron.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.summary: The sunshine vitamin: helps your gut take up calcium and keeps bones and muscles working. Found in: Mushrooms exposed to UV light (D2), Fortified plant milks and cereals, Vegan D3 from lichen (supplements).
items.why: Helps your body absorb calcium, so bones stay strong. Severe lack causes rickets in children and soft bones in adults (strong evidence). Supports muscle and immune function. Taking extra for general disease prevention has not held up: a large trial of over 25,000 adults found no drop in cancer or heart disease…
cautions: A blood test is the only way to know your level. Ask a clinician before taking high amounts: too much can raise blood calcium and harm the kidneys.
Check with a pharmacist if you take steroids, weight-loss medicines or anti-seizure drugs.

items.title: Vitamin E
items.summary: A fat-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes. Found in: Sunflower seeds, Almonds and hazelnuts, Wheat germ and wheat germ oil, Peanut butter.
items.why: Protects fats in your cell membranes from damage by free radicals (strong evidence it is needed). Supports the immune system. Taking vitamin E supplements has not been shown to prevent heart disease or cancer in large trials (moderate evidence of no benefit).
cautions: High-dose supplements can raise bleeding risk, especially with blood thinners. Ask a clinician or pharmacist first.
A large trial of vitamin E found a higher rate of prostate cancer in men taking it. Food is the safe route.

items.title: Vitamin K
items.summary: Makes the proteins that help blood clot, and others that direct calcium in bones. Found in: Kale, collards, spinach, turnip greens (K1), Broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage (K1), Natto, fermented soybeans, the richest K2 (MK-7) food, Parsley, scallions, lettuce.
items.why: Needed for blood clotting (strong evidence). Helps make proteins that bind calcium in bone. K2 specifically, for bone and artery health: studies so far are mixed and small, and whether K2 supplements prevent fractures or artery stiffening is not settled (mixed evidence).
cautions: If you take warfarin (Coumadin) or a similar blood thinner, vitamin K changes how it works. Keep your intake steady and ask your clinician before adding a supplement or changing how many greens you eat.

items.title: Zinc
items.summary: For immunity, wound healing, taste and smell. Found in: Pumpkin seeds, Chickpeas, lentils, beans, Cashews and hemp seeds, Oats and whole grains.
items.why: Needed for immune cells, wound healing, and your sense of taste and smell (strong evidence). Zinc lozenges started within a day of cold symptoms may shorten a cold slightly (mixed evidence).
cautions: Taking a lot for a long time can cause copper shortage and weaken immunity.
Zinc nasal sprays have been linked to lasting loss of smell. The US FDA warns against them.
Zinc can reduce absorption of some antibiotics. Ask a pharmacist.

items.title: 7 Days to More Fiber
items.summary: Small swaps toward 25 to 29 grams a day. 7 days.
items.why: Most adults eat about half the fiber linked to the biggest health benefits. One small, tasty swap a day, the science behind it, and a shopping list that builds itself.

items.title: 5 Days of Gratitude
items.summary: Notice the good and reach out to the people who matter. 5 days.
items.why: Five short practices from positive psychology: three good things, savoring, a thank-you to someone in your life, a loving-kindness meditation, and a plan to keep it going. The research suggests modest benefits for mood. About 5 to 7 minutes a day.

items.title: 5 Gentle Mornings
items.summary: Wake up your body in about 10 minutes a day. 5 days.
items.why: Five mornings, five ways to start the day: daylight, water, gentle movement and breath. No equipment, no gym, nothing strenuous. About 10 minutes each.

items.title: 10 Days of Yoga & Stretch
items.summary: Gentle mobility basics, about 10 minutes a day. 10 days.
items.why: Ten short sessions to loosen up and build an easy daily habit: morning stretches, gentle yoga, a desk reset, tai chi, qigong and a bedtime stretch. Nothing strenuous. If you've told us you have limited mobility, every routine switches to a seated version. About 7 to 10 minutes a day.

items.title: 7 Days to Relax
items.summary: A few minutes a day to retrain how you respond to stress. 7 days.
items.why: One short lesson a day. You'll learn why slow breathing works, practice the five most useful techniques, and finish knowing which one works best for you. About 5 minutes a day.

items.title: 7 Nights of Better Sleep
items.summary: Light, timing and a more relaxed wind-down, one habit a night. 7 days.
items.why: Seven short lessons on the habits most linked to better sleep: morning light, a caffeine cutoff, a wind-down routine, slow breathing in bed, a cool dark bedroom, parking your worries, and what sleep researchers teach about using your bed for sleep. This is education, not treatment. About 5 to 8 minutes a day.

items.title: Black bean tacos with avocado
items.summary: Fifteen minutes, crunchy slaw, no oven. 15 min.
items.why: Black beans have about 15 grams of fiber per cooked cup, and pulses lower LDL cholesterol in trials. Avocado adds mostly unsaturated fat, the kind linked to better heart health.
cautions: Canned beans, broth and sauces can be salty. Rinse beans and choose low-sodium versions if you're watching salt.
New to beans or lots of fiber? Start with smaller portions and drink water; your gut adjusts in a few weeks.

items.title: Ginger-turmeric red lentil dal
items.summary: Red lentils melt into a cozy, golden stew. 30 min.
items.why: The proven benefit here is from the lentils: pulses lower LDL cholesterol in trials. Ginger and turmeric add flavor; research on curcumin for inflammation is mixed and mostly uses supplements, so treat the spices as taste, not treatment. Black pepper and oil help the body absorb curcumin.
cautions: Turmeric and ginger here are normal cooking amounts. The Pantry's cautions about blood thinners and liver effects are about turmeric supplements, not food.
Leafy greens are high in vitamin K. If you take warfarin, keep how much you eat steady from week to week and tell your clinician.
New to beans or lots of fiber? Start with smaller portions and drink water; your gut adjusts in a few weeks.

items.title: Greek salad with chickpeas
items.summary: No cooking. A big bowl in about 15 minutes. 15 min.
items.why: This is a Mediterranean-style meal: vegetables, legumes and extra virgin olive oil. In the PREDIMED trial, a Mediterranean diet with extra olive oil lowered major cardiovascular events compared with a lower-fat diet.
cautions: Canned beans, broth and sauces can be salty. Rinse beans and choose low-sodium versions if you're watching salt.
Olives and feta are salty, so you may not need extra salt.

items.title: Burdock & carrot kinpira
items.summary: A classic Japanese side: sweet, salty and crunchy. 20 min.
items.why: Burdock is rich in inulin, a prebiotic fiber that feeds gut bacteria. Studies of burdock itself in people are few; the reliable benefit is the fiber, the same as other vegetables. Claims that it 'purifies the blood' aren't supported; your liver and kidneys do that job.
cautions: Buy burdock at a store, don't forage it: wild burdock can be confused with toxic plants.
Burdock may lower blood sugar. If you take diabetes medicine, watch your levels.
Soy sauce contains wheat; use tamari labelled gluten-free if needed.
Inulin can cause gas at first. Start with a small serving.

items.title: Weeknight lentil soup
items.summary: One pot, pantry staples, even better the next day. 30 min.
items.why: About one serving of beans, peas or lentils a day lowered LDL cholesterol in a meta-analysis of trials, and lentils bring protein and fiber together. Half the pot is vegetables, which matches the plate model.
cautions: Leafy greens are high in vitamin K. If you take warfarin, keep how much you eat steady from week to week and tell your clinician.
Canned beans, broth and sauces can be salty. Rinse beans and choose low-sodium versions if you're watching salt.
New to beans or lots of fiber? Start with smaller portions and drink water; your gut adjusts in a few weeks.

items.title: Quick minestrone
items.summary: Beans, greens and a little pasta in one pot. 30 min.
items.why: Eating more vegetables and fruit is linked to lower risk of heart disease and early death in a large meta-analysis, with benefits up to about 800 g a day. Beans and whole wheat pasta add fiber and protein.
cautions: Leafy greens are high in vitamin K. If you take warfarin, keep how much you eat steady from week to week and tell your clinician.
Canned beans, broth and sauces can be salty. Rinse beans and choose low-sodium versions if you're watching salt.

items.title: Miso soup with greens & shiitake
items.summary: Ten minutes to a warm, savory bowl. 10 min.
items.why: Miso is a fermented food. In a 10-week Stanford trial, eating more fermented foods increased gut microbiome diversity and lowered some inflammation markers. Cooking reduces live microbes, so stirring miso in off the heat keeps more of them; the evidence for miso specifically is limited.
cautions: Miso is very high in sodium. If you're watching salt, use less and add more mushrooms for flavor.
Leafy greens are high in vitamin K. If you take warfarin, keep how much you eat steady from week to week and tell your clinician.

items.title: Overnight oats with berries & chia
items.summary: Stir it together at night, grab it in the morning. 5 min.
items.why: Oats carry beta-glucan, the soluble fiber behind an FDA-authorized heart-health claim, and chia and berries add more fiber. Eating more fiber and whole grains is linked to lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes in large reviews. Yogurt with live cultures is a fermented food.
cautions: Oats are naturally gluten-free but often cross-contaminated. If you have celiac disease, buy oats labelled gluten-free.
Chia swells a lot in liquid; give it time to soak and drink water with it.

items.title: Sheet-pan salmon (or tofu) with greens
items.summary: Everything on one tray, about 25 minutes. 25 min.
items.why: Fatty fish like salmon is the richest food source of the omega-3s EPA and DHA. The American Heart Association recommends one to two seafood meals a week, based on lower cardiovascular risk in studies, and salmon is on the FDA's low-mercury 'best choices' list.
cautions: Contains fish. The tofu version contains soy instead.
Leafy greens are high in vitamin K. If you take warfarin, keep how much you eat steady from week to week and tell your clinician.

items.title: Roasted sweet potato & kale bowl
items.summary: Crispy chickpeas, quinoa and a lemony tahini drizzle. 30 min.
items.why: Built on the plate model: half vegetables, a quarter whole grains, a quarter protein, with olive oil. Chickpeas are a pulse, which lower LDL cholesterol in trials, and sweet potatoes are rich in beta-carotene and fiber.
cautions: Tahini is made from sesame.
Leafy greens are high in vitamin K. If you take warfarin, keep how much you eat steady from week to week and tell your clinician.
New to beans or lots of fiber? Start with smaller portions and drink water; your gut adjusts in a few weeks.

items.title: Veggie stir-fry with brown rice
items.summary: Use whatever vegetables are in the fridge. 25 min.
items.why: Swapping refined grains for whole grains like brown rice is linked to lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes in a large Lancet review. Tofu or edamame adds plant protein, and the plate is about half vegetables.
cautions: Soy sauce contains wheat; use tamari labelled gluten-free if needed.
Canned beans, broth and sauces can be salty. Rinse beans and choose low-sodium versions if you're watching salt.

items.why: Yogurt with live cultures is a fermented food, and walnuts and flaxseed are among the richest plant sources of omega-3 ALA. In the PREDIMED trial, a Mediterranean diet with daily nuts lowered cardiovascular events.
cautions: Contains tree nuts (walnuts).
Never give honey to babies under 12 months; it can cause infant botulism.

items.title: Tell us your goals
items.summary: Pick what you want most, how active you are, how much time you have, and anything we should know about your health.
items.why: Your daily plan, suggestions and safety notes are tailored to what you tell us.

items.title: Sign in and sync
items.summary: Create an account to back up your data and use Rooted on more than one device.
items.why: You won't lose your progress if you change phones.

items.title: Scan a product's additives
items.summary: Scan a barcode, type its number or paste an ingredient list to see the additives in a packaged food, what the research says about each, and how strong that research is. You can also flag allergens you avoid.
items.why: Labels list long names. Seeing what studies and regulators have found makes it easier to choose for yourself.

items.title: Animal products guide
items.summary: Learn how meat, milk and eggs are produced: antibiotics, hormones, feed additives, organic versus conventional, and what labels mean, with the research behind each and how solid it is.
items.why: Knowing what is and isn't regulated, and what the studies show, lets you choose by facts rather than marketing.

items.title: Home apothecary
items.summary: Simple teas and remedies from what you grow, with safety rules for each.
items.why: Some herbs have useful evidence behind them, and some interact with medicines. Both matter.

items.title: Bedtime routine
items.summary: Set your bedtime and wake time, pick a wind-down and sleep session, get a reminder, and track your streak.
items.why: A steady wind-down and a regular schedule are two of the best-supported sleep habits.

items.title: Blue Zones and healing places
items.summary: Explore the five places known for long lives, the nine habits they share, and nature spots that may help you feel better.
items.why: The habits of long-lived communities are simple and borrowable.

items.title: Breath test (BOLT)
items.summary: Time how long you can comfortably pause after a normal exhale, and track it week to week.
items.why: A simple number to see whether your everyday breathing is getting more relaxed over time.

items.title: Inside your brain
items.summary: An illustrated guide to brain regions, brainwaves, hearing, sleep and what the evidence says about sound.
items.why: Knowing how your brain works helps you judge wellness claims for yourself.

items.title: Breathing techniques
items.summary: Box breathing, 4-7-8, the physiological sigh, coherent and power breathing, each with when to use it and the evidence.
items.why: Different patterns suit different moments, like panic, focus or falling asleep.

items.title: Breathing reminders
items.summary: Pick times of day and add daily breathing reminders to your phone's calendar.
items.why: A reminder at the right moment turns a good intention into a habit.

items.title: Before and after check-ins
items.summary: Rate your stress before and after a session and see which techniques help you most.
items.why: Your own results are a better guide than anyone's general advice.

items.title: Chimes, voice or tone
items.summary: Choose how a breathing session guides you: chimes, a spoken voice, a tone or silence, with optional rain or stream sounds.
items.why: Being guided by sound lets you close your eyes and stop watching the screen.

items.title: Bring it home checklist
items.summary: Tick off small weekly ways to bring a healing place into ordinary life, and schedule a nature walk.
items.why: You don't need a retreat. A little every week adds up.

items.title: Build your own session
items.summary: Pick a carrier tone, beat, noise and layers, name it, and save it.
items.why: Tuning a session to your own ears makes it more pleasant to use.

items.title: Health calendar
items.summary: Schedule walks, breathing, meals and appointments, repeat them, and check them off.
items.why: Habits with a set time are far more likely to happen.

items.title: Send to Apple or Google
items.summary: Send events to Apple, Google or Outlook with a 5-minute reminder, or, when signed in, subscribe with a live link.
items.why: Reminders show up where you already look every day.

items.title: Circles
items.summary: Do a program with up to 12 friends or family: see each other's days done and send cheers.
items.why: Gentle company and a little accountability help habits stick. Only first names and days done are shared.

items.title: Combos
items.summary: Short guided flows that stack breath, movement, light and reflection, like Morning Armor, Evening Reset and Gentle Reset.
items.why: Linking a few small habits into one routine makes each one easier to keep.

items.title: Help now
items.summary: Crisis lines to call or text any time. The heart button at the top of every page opens them too.
items.why: When things are really hard, talking to someone right away matters most.

items.title: Today's plan
items.summary: Home shows a few small things picked for your goals and the time of day, and checks them off as you go.
items.why: A short, specific list is easier to start than a whole app full of choices.

items.title: Inside your gut
items.summary: Follow a bite through your body, see how fiber works, and why a walk after meals flattens blood sugar.
items.why: Understanding the why makes small food changes feel worth it.

items.title: Plan your garden
items.summary: Tell us your space and light, get herbs and vegetables that suit it, and track what you've planted.
items.why: Growing even a few herbs gets you outside, moving and eating fresher food.

items.title: Good deeds log
items.summary: Jot down kind things you did and see how many this week, with ideas when you're stuck.
items.why: Kindness is linked with better mood for the giver, too.

items.title: Gratitude journal
items.summary: Write down three good things from today and keep a private streak.
items.why: Noticing good moments is linked with small but real lifts in mood.

items.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
items.summary: A step-by-step walk through five things you see, four you feel, three you hear, two you smell and one you taste.
items.why: Turning attention to your senses can interrupt a spiral of worry or panic.

items.title: Healing Frequencies sessions
items.summary: Binaural beat sessions for sleep, focus and relaxation, generated live in your browser.
items.why: Many people find steady, gentle sound helps them relax or focus. Evidence is mixed, and we say so.

items.title: Camera heart check
items.summary: Rest a fingertip on your phone's camera to estimate your heart rate and see it respond to slow breathing.
items.why: Watching your heart slow down shows you the effect is real. It's an estimate, not a medical test.

items.title: Invite a friend
items.summary: Send a friend a link to join you, or to do a program together.
items.why: Doing a habit with someone else makes it more likely you'll both keep it.

items.title: My journey
items.summary: A private page that shows how you've grown, from Seed to Ancient grove, and the special symbols you can earn.
items.why: Seeing your own progress can help you keep going. It counts days you showed up, never streaks, and it's never shared.

items.title: Privacy, terms and disclaimer
items.summary: Plain-language privacy policy, terms of use, and a health disclaimer.
items.why: Know exactly what Rooted does with your information, and what it isn't.

items.title: Light box timer
items.summary: Time a morning light session, outdoors or with a light box.
items.why: Bright morning light helps set your body clock, which can improve sleep and mood.

items.title: Your light day
items.summary: A timeline of when to get bright light and when to keep it dim, based on your wake time.
items.why: Bright days and dark nights are the simplest way to work with your body clock.

items.title: Meditation timer
items.summary: A quiet timer with a gentle bell, plus a diagram of what stillness changes in your body under stress.
items.why: Regular short sits are linked with lower stress for many people.

items.title: How are you today?
items.summary: Tap one of five faces on Home to check in. A low day gently surfaces support.
items.why: Noticing how you feel, day to day, helps you see patterns and what's helping.

items.title: Follow-along routines
items.summary: Press play on an after-meal walk, a desk reset, yoga, tai chi or qigong, with animated figures to follow.
items.why: Seeing each move makes it easy to do it right, with no class or equipment.

items.title: Muscle map
items.summary: See which muscles each routine reaches, highlighted on a body diagram.
items.why: Knowing what a routine works helps you pick one for how your body feels today.

items.title: My Stuff
items.summary: Your saved list, sessions you've built, what you were listening to, and reminders.
items.why: Everything you like, in one place.

items.title: Your nature dose
items.summary: Slide to your minutes outdoors this week and see how close you are to about two hours.
items.why: Research links roughly two hours a week in nature with better health and wellbeing.

items.title: Night light and sunrise
items.summary: Turn your screen into a dim amber night light, or a slow red-to-white sunrise for waking up.
items.why: Warm, dim light at night disturbs your body clock the least.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals guide
items.summary: Look up any vitamin or mineral, including magnesium, vitamin D with K2 and iron: what it does, which fruits, vegetables and other foods are rich in it, who tends to run low, and how strong the research is.
items.why: Knowing what each nutrient does, and where to find it, makes eating well simpler than guessing at supplements.

items.title: One-minute settle-in
items.summary: Follow a growing and shrinking circle, breathing in for 4 and out for 6. Quick picks below it start the right pattern for panic, sleep, focus or energy.
items.why: Slow breathing with a longer exhale is one of the quickest ways to settle a racing body.

items.title: Pantry and body map
items.summary: Look up foods, herbs and spices, see where in the body the research suggests they may help, and how strong the evidence is.
items.why: Honest evidence ratings help you spend on food that's worth it.

items.title: Build a breath pattern
items.summary: Set your own counts for breathing in, holding, breathing out and resting, then save it.
items.why: A pattern that feels comfortable to you is one you'll actually use.

items.title: Plan my day
items.summary: Let Rooted fit a few small practices into the free gaps in your day.
items.why: It does the fitting-in for you, so a busy day still has room to breathe.

items.title: Plate builder
items.summary: Tap foods to build a plate and compare it with the Healthy Eating Plate.
items.why: A simple picture of a balanced meal is easier to follow than counting.

items.title: Footprint pledges
items.summary: Pledge small habits that lighten your footprint, with an honest impact rating on each.
items.why: Acting on what you care about is linked with a sense of purpose.

items.title: Muscle relaxation
items.summary: A guided round of tensing and then releasing each muscle group.
items.why: Feeling the contrast teaches your body what letting go of tension feels like.

items.title: Profile picture
items.summary: Pick a healing symbol (crystal, tree, wave, lotus and more) or add your own photo.
items.why: Makes the app feel like yours. Photos stay on your device and are never shown to friends.

items.title: Profiles
items.summary: Add a profile for each person in your home so plans, logs and lists stay separate.
items.why: Everyone gets suggestions that fit them.

items.title: Daily programs
items.summary: Multi-day programs, like 7 Days to Relax or 5 Gentle Mornings, with one short lesson a day.
items.why: A day-by-day path removes the guesswork about what to do next.

items.title: Pantry recipes
items.summary: Simple meals from pantry staples, with steps, timing and a button to schedule cooking.
items.why: Cooking at home is one of the easiest ways to eat more fiber and less sugar.

items.title: Frequency safety guide
items.summary: Safe volumes, flashing light, low frequencies, headphones and common myths about sound.
items.why: Listening safely protects your hearing and keeps sessions comfortable.

items.title: Safety plan
items.summary: Write down your warning signs, what helps, and who to call, ready for hard moments. Private to this device.
items.why: Safety plans are recommended by crisis professionals because they help in the moment.

items.title: Share cards
items.summary: Make a picture of your week or a finished program to share or save.
items.why: Sharing a win with a friend can help you stick with it.

items.title: Shopping list
items.summary: Add pantry items to a list grouped by store aisle, check them off as you shop, and plan a grocery trip.
items.why: A list made while you're thinking about health keeps the good stuff in your cart.

items.title: Shows
items.summary: Longer multi-part listening series you can play in order.
items.why: A series gives you something to come back to each day.

items.title: Better sleep guide
items.summary: How your sleep clock works, plus morning, evening, caffeine, temperature and nap habits.
items.why: Small, well-supported changes often help more than any gadget.

items.title: Sound bath
items.summary: Strike singing bowls, chimes and a gong, or let a sound bath play by itself. All synthesized live.
items.why: Many people find it a relaxing focus point for rest or meditation.

items.title: Mix your sound
items.summary: In the full-screen player, add music, nature sounds or a solfeggio tone, set a sleep timer, and check your headphones.
items.why: The right mix is the one you enjoy enough to keep listening to.

items.title: Store finder
items.summary: See which kinds of shops carry what's on your list, and open a map search for ones near you.
items.why: Knowing where to go saves a wasted trip.

items.title: Therapy and bodywork
items.summary: Therapies with good evidence, how to find a therapist, questions to ask, and what massage, acupuncture and more can and can't do.
items.why: Knowing your options makes it easier to take the first step toward care.

items.title: Water tracker
items.summary: Tap to log glasses of water and watch the glass fill toward your daily goal.
items.why: Many people drink less than they think. A quick tap makes it visible.

items.title: Your week
items.summary: A recap of your minutes, sessions, mood, water and calendar over the last seven days.
items.why: Seeing progress, even small, keeps you going.

items.title: Import your work calendar
items.summary: Bring in meetings and shifts from a calendar file as gray busy blocks, so plans fit around them. They stay on this device.
items.why: Seeing health plans beside real commitments keeps them realistic.

items.title: Worried about someone
items.summary: What to say, what to avoid, and how to help someone who's struggling.
items.why: Asking directly and listening well can make a real difference.

items.title: Your data
items.summary: See what's kept, download it, back up private notes if you choose, or delete it all.
items.why: Your health data is yours. You stay in control of it.
